amendments.rule: An English function word the ASV supplies for an adverbial accusative belongs to the noun whose case-function licenses it — *as a bird*, *to your mountain* — and is never `added`. **An appositional or measure nominal the ASV introduces with a supplied preposition is read the same way.** Where a noun or numeral stands in the clause with no preposition and no object marker on it, and the ASV writes an *of* or a *for* before it to state what that nominal contributes, the word is that nominal's own rendering: `אֹרֶךְ חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף` → *the length ... of five and twenty thousand*, `תֹּכֶן אֶחָד` → *of one measure*, `לַאֲחֻזָּה עֶשְׂרִים לְשָׁכֹת` → *for a possession ..., for twenty chambers*, `חַטָּאת שְׂעִיר עִזִּים` → *a he goat ... for a sin offering*. It goes to the word it stands before, which is the noun or numeral opening that phrase, and the unit still heads on the word carrying the lexeme under rules 24 and 31; the supplied preposition is never the head. **Read *an *of* or a *for** as any preposition the ASV writes for the nominal's own contribution, and not as a closed list.** What licenses the word is that a bare nominal stands in the clause and the English needs a word to say what it contributes there, so read the condition and not the lemma, exactly as rule 40 does for the preposition it silences: a comparative *as* before a nominal the ASV construes as a comparison — `פַּלְגֵי מַיִם` → ***as*** *the watercourses* — an agent *by* before a bare nominal the ASV construes with a passive participle — `מְבַקְשֵׁי מָוֶת` → *driven to and fro* ***by*** *them that seek death* — and a *with* or an *in* before a nominal standing in a `מִן` comparison — `אֵשֶׁת מִדְיָנִים` → ***with*** *a contentious woman*, `בֵּית חָבֶר` → ***in*** *a wide house* — all go to the nominal on the same terms as an *of* or a *for*, and this rule's first sentence already writes *as* and *to* for the adverbial accusative. Three limits, each stated where it belongs. A word an object marker stands to take is the marker's under rule 16, and an *as for* the ASV writes before a topicalized phrase no marker and no preposition stands on is `added` under that rule rather than this one, since a nominal's fronting is not a case-function. A preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own bare object is the verb's under rule 44, and this rule's own closing paragraph disposes of one a predicate's valency needs. And a coordinating or subordinating connective the ASV writes beside such a phrase is not a word spent on the nominal at all: rules 14 and 55 count those against the morphemes that could carry them. **A preposition standing elsewhere in the clause that has already taken an English word of its own does not make such a word a surplus.** Rule 52's count governs two English words offered to one morpheme, and here each phrase has a rendering of its own, so a written `לְ` rendered *for a possession* does not silence the *for* the ASV writes before the phrase standing beside it. **But an English preposition the ASV writes again over a member the Hebrew coordinates under one written preposition is that preposition's, and not the bare nominal's.** Hebrew gaps a preposition in the later members of a coordination where English rewrites it, and the word the ASV writes there is the distributed scope of the one written morpheme: it joins that morpheme's possibly discontinuous unit under rule 25, however much stands between and whatever word the ASV chose for the members in between. `בְּכֹל מַלְכֵי יְהוּדָה וַאֲשֶׁר הָיוּ לְפָנָיו` → *among all the kings of Judah, nor* ***among*** *them that were before him* gives the second *among* to the one `בְּ`, and `בַּחְלַח וּבְחָבוֹר נְהַר גּוֹזָן וְעָרֵי מָדָי` → *in Halah and on the Habor the river of Gozan and* ***in*** *the cities of the Medes* gives the third preposition to the first `בְּ`, across the second member's own `בְּ` holding the *on* written for it. What tells this from the preceding sentences is order and repetition together, not that the nominal is bare: this sentence governs a member coordinated after a written preposition of its own phrase whose English the ASV has simply written again, and the earlier sentences govern a nominal standing before any such preposition, or in a phrase where none is written at all. So read whether a preposition of that phrase stands earlier in the coordination before giving the word to the noun — `הַנִּמְצָא בֵית־יְהוָה וּבְאֹצְרוֹת בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ` → *that was found* ***in*** *the house of Jehovah, and in the treasures of the king's house* leaves its first *in* to `בַּיִת` under this rule's first sentence, because the written `בְּ` stands after it and nothing is being repeated. Test by subtraction as elsewhere: ask whether the English word states what a bare nominal contributes to its clause, or restates a relation a written preposition already carries over that member. **But the noun must be present.** Where the ASV supplies the head noun as well as the function word, no morpheme is there to carry either, and the whole supplied phrase is its own `added` unit under rule 30: `חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת בַּחֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת` → *five hundred* ***in length*** *by five hundred* ***in breadth*** supplies both the preposition and the dimension noun in a clause whose Hebrew names neither, exactly as the italic ***reeds*** of `חֲמִשָּׁה וְעֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף` supplies a measure noun. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the English and ask whether a Hebrew noun standing in the clause has lost the relation it bears, or whether what has gone is a noun the Hebrew never wrote. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it either way and decides nothing, by rule 7. **And a bare noun that completes a predicate's own valency is not an adverbial accusative at all.** Where a verb or a predicate adjective governs a bare noun as its complement — no preposition and no object marker on it — and the English predicate can reach that complement only through a preposition the ASV has written, that word answers to the predicate's valency and joins the predicate's unit under rule 44, while the noun keeps its own English: `מָלֵאתָ` → *thou art full* ***of*** *the judgment* and `מָלֵא דָשֶׁן` → *would be full* ***of*** *fatness* both give the *of* to `מָלֵא`, headed on *full*, and leave `דִין` and `דֶשֶׁן` their own words. Decide it by asking whether the ASV had a relation to choose: where the English predicate admits no other word before such a complement — *full of* is the only way English writes it — the preposition is the predicate's, and where the word states what the noun contributes to the clause and another would have served, this rule governs and the word is the noun's, as it does for `יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר` → *distil* ***in*** *rain* and `כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ` → *mighty* ***in*** *strength*. Read the English predicate rather than where the noun stands, since Hebrew writes such a complement before its predicate as readily as after it, and JOB.36.16 and JOB.36.17 are the two shapes in one chapter. **But run the direct-object question before that test, because the test cannot answer it.** Where the bare noun is the direct object of a verb standing in the clause, rule 44's supplied-preposition clause governs and the word joins that verb's unit, headed on the lexical verb, whatever preposition the ASV chose and whether or not another would have served. A recasting that makes a transitive Hebrew verb intransitive in English always leaves the translator a relation to choose, so the availability of another word says nothing about which morpheme licenses the one written, and only what governs the noun in the Hebrew can tell the two apart. `וְיוֹסֶף לֶקַח` → *he will increase* ***in*** *learning* and `מְיַשְּׁרִים אֹרְחוֹתָם` → *go right* ***on*** *their ways* both give the word to the verb, because `לֶקַח` and `אֹרַח` are what those verbs govern, and rule 44's own examples — *have done violence to my law*, *hast greedily gained of thy neighbors* — are the same construction written without the recasting. What the preceding sentence governs is a complement no verb takes as its object: the accusative of manner of `יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר`, the accusative of specification of `כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ`, and the `מָלֵא` case, where an adjective and not a verb is the predicate. Read MACULA's clause for what governs the noun, as this rule's third limit already directs in deferring to rule 44, and where no verb governs it the preceding sentences stand as before.
amendments.why: PRO.9 wrote the same construction twice — a bare Hebrew direct object the ASV reaches through a supplied preposition, in a recasting that makes the English predicate intransitive — and the chapter analysed it two ways: *go right on their ways* (9.15) under rule 44, *increase in learning* (9.9) under rule 33. The misleading sentence is rule 33's own 'whether the ASV had a relation to choose' test, which passes for both cases and so decides neither; rule 33's third limit and rule 44's closing limit both already say a verb's bare object is rule 44's, so the correction belongs in the paragraph that misled rather than as a new rule pointing back at it. The amendment adds nothing to the doctrine of either rule; it names the question that has to be run first and the reason the existing test cannot substitute for it, and it keeps the מָלֵא, מָטָר and כֹּחַ examples explicitly on rule 33's side.

conventions: A preposition the ASV supplies to reach the bare direct object of a Hebrew verb joins the verb's unit under rule 44, not the noun's under rule 33, even where the ASV's recasting makes the English predicate intransitive and the object an English adjunct: וְיוֹסֶף לֶקַח -> *he will increase in learning* (9.9) and מְיַשְּׁרִים אֹרְחוֹתָם -> *go right on their ways* (9.15) both give the word to the verb, headed on the lexical verb. Rule 33's 'another would have served' test does not decide such a case, because a transitive Hebrew verb recast intransitively always leaves a relation to choose; read what governs the noun in the Hebrew instead. Rule 33 still governs a complement no verb takes as its object.

מְרֹמֵי קָרֶת stands in both 9.3 and 9.14, and what מְרֹמֵי holds follows the outer construct noun. In 9.3 the three-level chain גַּפֵּי מְרֹמֵי קָרֶת is split so that each noun holds an English word of its own — גַּפֵּי takes *the highest* with the phrase's supplied *the* under rule 29, מְרֹמֵי takes *places* — rather than fusing the pair and marking one of them unrepresented, which rules 2 and 30 both refuse. In 9.14 no second construct noun stands before מְרֹמֵי, so it holds the whole *in the high places*, the *in* being the construct relation of כִּסֵּא recast under rule 19 and the head falling on *high* under rule 31. The head difference between the two verses is the consequence of that division, not a second judgment.

amended.why: PRO.9 wrote the same construction twice — a bare Hebrew direct object the ASV reaches through a supplied preposition, in a recasting that makes the English predicate intransitive — and the chapter analysed it two ways: *go right on their ways* (9.15) under rule 44, *increase in learning* (9.9) under rule 33. The misleading sentence is rule 33's own 'whether the ASV had a relation to choose' test, which passes for both cases and so decides neither; rule 33's third limit and rule 44's closing limit both already say a verb's bare object is rule 44's, so the correction belongs in the paragraph that misled rather than as a new rule pointing back at it. The amendment adds nothing to the doctrine of either rule; it names the question that has to be run first and the reason the existing test cannot substitute for it, and it keeps the מָלֵא, מָטָר and כֹּחַ examples explicitly on rule 33's side.

report: One genuine cross-verse split, in a shape the candidate table could not show because the two sides are aligned units of different lemmas: a preposition the ASV supplies to reach a Hebrew verb's bare direct object. PRO.9.15 gives the *on* of מְיַשְּׁרִים אֹרְחוֹתָם -> *go right on their ways* to the verb under rule 44; PRO.9.9 gave the *in* of וְיוֹסֶף לֶקַח -> *he will increase in learning* to the noun under rule 33. Both nouns are bare direct objects of a transitive verb, with no object marker and no preposition of their own, and nothing in the source distinguishes them.

Resolved toward rule 44, because rule 33's own third limit already defers there ('A preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own bare object is the verb's under rule 44'), and rule 44's limit tells you to read which the Hebrew noun is. Rule 33's examples are complements no verb governs — the accusative of manner of יָזֹקּוּ מָטָר, the accusative of specification of כַּבִּיר כֹּחַ, and the adjectival *full of*. PRO.9.9 is patched: t021 *in* moves into the יוֹסֵף unit, head unchanged on *increase* per rule 44, and לֶקַח keeps only *learning*. PRO.9.15 stands as accepted.

The 'would another have served' test in rule 33's closing paragraph is what misled the PRO.9.9 pass: a recasting that makes a transitive Hebrew verb intransitive in English always leaves a relation to choose, so that test cannot separate the two cases. Amendment to rule 33 returned, sharpening that paragraph rather than adding a cross-referencing new rule.

Checked and found licensed rather than split: מָרוֹם in 9.3 vs 9.14 (a second construct noun, גַּפֵּי, holds *the highest* in 9.3, and nothing stands before מְרֹמֵי in 9.14); בַּיִת in 9.1 vs 9.14 (head noun with suffix vs rectum of פֶּתַח); בִּינָה in 9.6 vs 9.10 (rectum vs predicate noun with copula); דֶּרֶךְ in 9.6 vs 9.15; בְּ in 9.5 vs 9.6 and the waws of 9.13 vs 9.18 (different English words the ASV wrote); the four לְ before an object adjective in 9.7, 9.8 and 9.9 (unrepresented where the ASV writes a bare object, aligned to *to* where it writes the word).

The table is blind to added units, so the dump was read end to end for them. The two *As for* runs in 9.4 and 9.16 are added in both verses, each one two-word unit headed on *As*, and no marker or preposition stands on either fronted phrase; the supplied object noun of 9.9, the supplied object pronoun of 9.12 and the supplied participle of 9.17 are added in all three; the italic *getteth* of 9.7 is folded into לֹקֵחַ because the Hebrew writes that verb in the first colon, and the italic *She* of 9.13 into אֵשֶׁת because the verse writes that referent. That is rule 34's and rule 25's boundary applied consistently in both directions.

BSB: no genuine error among the five. The three לְ (9.7, 9.8, 9.9) are the documented convention difference — the ASV writes bare English objects and rule 40 silences the preposition, while BSB attaches it to its phrase. The 9.16 waw is this chapter's count of two waws against the ASV's single *And*, which stands where the first waw's colon opens, so the second is unrendered under rule 14. The 9.12 suffix of לְבַדְּךָ is a real tie, named in that verse's note under rule 8: one English *thou* answers to both the suffix and the finite verb's person, and the chapter gives it to the verb. Left as accepted; a BSB rate is not a reason to move an edge.
